procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (whose name is not explicitly mentioned but is represented by S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Adv., et al.) appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's Judgment and Order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, seemingly based on a defect in the charge framed by the Special Court regarding the alleged demand for illegal gratification. The Supreme Court noted the Special Court omitted to frame a specific charge on demand allegedly made by the appellant on 6th and 13th August 2004 and acceptance thereof on 13th August 2004.

issue.issue_text: Whether the omission to frame a specific charge for the alleged demands on 6th and 13th August 2004, and the framing of a defective charge, caused a failure of justice and prejudiced the appellant's right to a fair defence under Section 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

facts: The appellant argued that the charge framed against him was defective and that there was an omission to frame a specific charge for the alleged demands for a bribe on 6th and 13th August 2004.
The charge that was framed incorrectly referred to a demand made on 12th July 2004, a date on which even the prosecution did not allege a demand was made.
The appellant contended that this defective charge and omission caused grave prejudice to him, as he could not defend himself properly.
The Supreme Court acknowledged that the Special Court had indeed omitted to frame a proper charge and that the charge as framed was "per se defective" and had been framed "very casually".
law: The Court relied on Section 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC).

Under this section, an omission to frame a charge or any error within a charge is not considered fatal to the prosecution's case unless the court believes that it has, in fact, resulted in a "failure of justice."
For an error in the charge to be fatal, the accused must establish that it caused prejudice to their right to a fair defence.
application: The Court examined the trial record, particularly the cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses (including PW-3) conducted by the appellant's advocate.
Based on this review, the Court found that the appellant had "clearly understood the prosecution case" concerning the demands allegedly made on 6th and 13th August 2004.
The fact that the appellant's defence was able to effectively cross-examine witnesses on these specific allegations demonstrated that he was aware of the case he had to meet.
Therefore, the Court reasoned that despite the clear defect and omission in the charge, the appellant was not actually prejudiced in his right to defend himself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that while the charge was indeed defective, this error was not fatal to the case. The Court held that no failure of justice had occurred because the appellant had clearly understood the allegations against him and was not prejudiced in his ability to mount a defence, as required by Section 464 of the CrPC.

appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that there was a failure to frame a proper and specific charge for the offence punishable under Section 7.

The appellant contended that the omission to frame a charge regarding the specific demands on 6th and 13th August 2004, and the framing of a defective charge, prejudiced their right to a fair defence and caused a failure of justice.

cases.principle: For establishing the commission of an offence punishable under Section 7.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A demand for gratification can be established even on the basis of circumstantial evidence.
obiter: It is well settled that for establishing the commission of an offence punishable under Section 7.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court did not render a specific finding on whether the defective charge caused a failure of justice under Section 464 of the CrPC. Instead, it found the issue moot because it allowed the appeal on a more fundamental, substantive ground: the prosecution's complete failure to establish the essential elements of the offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act. The court concluded that since there was no evidence, circumstantial or otherwise, to prove the demand for gratification, the conviction could not be sustained, making an analysis of the procedural defect in the charge unnecessary.
legal_tests_applied: For establishing the commission of an offence punishable under Section 7 of the PC Act, proof of demand of gratification and acceptance of the gratification is a sine qua non.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument regarding the defective charge was not the basis for the final decision. The court did not engage with the question of whether prejudice was caused under Section 464 CrPC because it found a more dispositive reason to acquit, namely the lack of evidence to prove the core element of 'demand'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent prevailed on this specific procedural point only in the sense that the court did not find the defective charge to be the reason for overturning the conviction. The court bypassed this argument and did not rule that the charge defect was fatal to the prosecution's case.
policy_considerations: Apart from the duty of the Trial Court, even the public prosecutor has a duty to be vigilant, and if a proper charge is not framed, it is his duty to apply to the Court to frame an appropriate charge.
